meta.blurb: Nadia writes twelve new rules to fix her family's whole life, and by Friday nobody has kept one. Then a retired nurse next door says to start much smaller. A glass of water at breakfast is where one busy family begins.
meta.bible: Nadia: a busy mother and bookkeeper, determined but often tired. Ben: her husband, a teacher, kind and a little disorganised. Theo: their son, ten years old, tired at school, later a runner. Ivy: their daughter, six years old, who loves charts, stars and dancing and refuses Broccoli. Mrs Obi: the retired School nurse next door, calm and wise, who gives general advice over the Garden fence. The Carter family lives in an ordinary town, and the book follows one school year from September to July. Key terms: Habit, Routine, Breakfast, Porridge, Sugar, Fluoride, Toothpaste, Dentist, Vaccines, Portions, Vegetables, Sunscreen, Bedtime, Handwashing, Stress, Willpower, Calendar, Plan B. Facts used, all hedged: a well-known study found a new habit took about two months on average with a very wide range; school-age children usually need about nine to twelve hours of sleep and adults seven or more; children are usually advised about an hour of activity a day and adults about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; many guidelines suggest about five portions of fruit and vegetables a day; dentists advise brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste. Voice: warm, encouraging, practical and a little humorous; no shame, no diagnosis, no personal medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Every school morning in the Carter house feels like a race that nobody has trained for. Nadia finds one shoe, Ben looks for his keys, and Theo and Ivy leave without breakfast.
One tired evening, Nadia decides that the whole family must become healthy overnight. She writes twelve new rules on a sheet of paper and sticks it to the fridge.
By Friday the list on the fridge has been forgotten, and everyone is tired and cross. The family orders pizza, and Nadia feels that she has failed.
Their neighbour Mrs Obi, a retired school nurse, has watched the week from over the fence. She says that big plans often fail, and that small changes usually last longer.
Mrs Obi explains that a habit is an action we repeat so often that it becomes almost automatic. The brain likes this, because it saves energy and attention for harder things.
Habits attach themselves to a time and a place, Mrs Obi says. Every day when Ivy gets home from school, her hand goes to the biscuit tin without any thought.
Mrs Obi tells Nadia to take down the long list and choose just one step. It should be so small that it feels almost silly to skip it.
That evening the Carters talk it over and agree on a first step. Everyone will drink a glass of water with breakfast, and nothing else will change yet.
Mrs Obi suggests tying the new step to something the family already does every morning. They always pour cereal, so now they will pour a glass of water straight afterwards.
Ben learns that the easier a step is, the more likely it is to happen. Each night he fills a jug and puts it on the table, ready for the morning.
The first week is not perfect, because Theo and Ivy forget the water on three mornings. The new habit is still weak, and it needs time to grow.
Ivy draws a chart with seven boxes and puts a gold star in one for every glass of water. Seeing the stars grow makes the whole family want to fill the chart.

Mrs Obi tells Nadia about a well-known study that followed people as they built a new habit. On average, people needed about two months before a new action felt automatic, although the time varied enormously from person to person.
Once the water habit has settled, Nadia adds a second small step. On Sunday nights she plans a simple breakfast, so that the school mornings feel calmer and nobody leaves the house hungry.
Nadia counts how many sweet drinks the children have in an ordinary week. Fruit juice and fizzy drinks contain a lot of sugar, so the family begins to choose water or milk more often.
On Thursday the whole family forgets the water, and one box on the chart stays empty. Nadia tells Ivy that one missed day does not spoil anything, as long as they start again tomorrow.
At parents' evening, Theo's teacher tells Nadia that he often yawns and looks tired in class. Nadia realises that Theo goes to bed late and has trouble getting up in the morning.
Nadia reads that children of Theo's age usually need between nine and twelve hours of sleep. Adults such as Nadia and Ben generally need at least seven hours every night.
The Carters build a bedtime routine that follows the same order every night. First comes a bath, then teeth, then a story, and finally the light goes out.
Bright screens late in the evening can make it harder for some people to fall asleep. So at eight o'clock the family puts every phone and tablet in a basket in the hall.
Adults need sleep too, so Nadia and Ben decide to go to bed fifteen minutes earlier each week. They stop when they feel rested, and they do not try to change everything at once.
After one bad night, Theo is worried that he will be tired all week. Nadia tells him that bodies recover, and that the best plan is to keep the usual routine.
On Tuesdays and Thursdays the Carters leave the car at home and walk to school. It takes only twenty minutes, and the children talk and laugh all the way.
Nadia reads that children are usually advised to be active for about an hour a day. Adults are usually advised to do about 150 minutes of moderate activity every week, and any movement counts.
After dinner, the Carters push back the furniture and put on music. Each night one person chooses the game, and Ivy always chooses dancing.
Rain is the enemy of every outdoor habit, so Nadia writes a plan B on the fridge. On wet days the family does star jumps, stretches and a funny walk through the house.
Ivy decides that she hates broccoli, and the plate goes back to the kitchen untouched. Nadia wants to insist, but she remembers that pressure at the table often makes children like a food even less.
Mrs Obi explains that many children need to meet a new food again and again before they accept it. So Nadia keeps putting a small piece on Ivy's plate and says nothing if it stays there.
On Saturday the children help to make the supper. Theo cuts the cucumber with a safe knife, Ivy washes the tomatoes, and both of them want to taste the result.
Many health guidelines suggest eating about five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. The family turns it into a game, and everyone tries to put four different colours on their plate.
Nadia puts a full fruit bowl in the middle of the table and moves the sweets to a high cupboard. People tend to eat what is easy to see and easy to reach, even when they are not very hungry.

The Carters begin to eat supper together at the table on most evenings, with every phone in the basket. Studies link shared meals with children's wellbeing, although it is hard to prove that the meals alone cause the benefits.
Weekday evenings are the hardest, so on Sunday Nadia cooks a large pot of soup and a tray of vegetables. Ben fills boxes and puts them in the fridge, ready for the busy days.
At the winter holidays there is a lot of rich food and many late nights. The Carters decide to enjoy themselves without guilt, and to return to their small habits in January.
In January work is very busy, and Nadia notices that she is snapping at the children. She tries three slow breaths before she answers, which can help the body to calm down a little.
At supper, the Carters ask each other a simple question about the day. Everyone shares one good thing and one hard thing, and the others listen without giving advice.
Washing hands with soap helps to stop germs from spreading. The family washes before meals and after using the toilet, and the children sing a short song to wash for long enough.
Dentists advise brushing teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste. Ivy gets a little chart for her teeth, and the whole family visits the dentist for a check-up.
As spring turns to summer, the family learns to protect their skin from the sun. They look for shade at midday, wear hats, and put on sun cream before they go out.

Nadia writes the children's check-ups in the family calendar, using a different colour for them. She follows the advice of the local doctor or nurse about vaccines, because they know the plan for their country.
The family sits down together to make a plan for daytime screens. The children help to write the rules, and the parents agree to follow them as well.
In March a heavy cold takes over the house, and every healthy habit disappears for a week. Mrs Obi tells them that restarting is easier than starting, as long as the first step is tiny.
The Carters realise that their home can help them or hold them back. They put walking shoes by the door, a water bottle on each school bag and a ball where everybody can see it.
A healthy family does not need to spend a lot of money. Frozen vegetables, dried beans, oats and tinned tomatoes are cheap, and they can be just as nourishing as fresh food.
Nadia notices that Ivy is copying everything the adults do, from drinking water to putting on shoes. Children learn from what they see, so the parents try to show the habits they hope for.
In spring Theo sees a poster for a children's fun run in July, and he decides to take part. Nadia helps him to plan short, easy runs that grow a little longer each week.
Theo puts a green tick on the calendar after every run, and soon the whole family wants ticks too. The calendar shows progress, but nobody worries about gaps.
Mrs Obi reminds Nadia that habits cannot solve everything. Illness, money worries and shift work all affect health, and anyone with a real concern should talk to a doctor.
In July Theo runs the fun run in the park, and the whole family cheers at the finish. Nadia sees that no single change was big, but together they have made a different year.

Mrs Obi says that the next step is always one more small change, and that kindness to yourself matters most. This book is general information and it is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: In the Carter house, every school morning arrived like a small storm, with lost shoes, missing homework and a toaster that seemed to burn the one slice nobody wanted. Nadia, the mother, stood in the middle of it all holding a hairbrush in one hand and a car key in the other, while Ben searched the sofa for his phone. By the time the front door finally slammed, ten-year-old Theo and six-year-old Ivy had left for school with no real breakfast at all.

After another rushed week, Nadia sat at the kitchen table and decided that the whole family would become healthy at once. She wrote twelve firm rules on a large sheet of paper, covering food, sleep, exercise and screens, and fixed it to the fridge with a magnet. It felt wonderfully decisive, and she went to bed that night quite certain that by Monday everything in the house would be different.

By Friday, the list on the fridge had become a kind of reproach, a page of good intentions that nobody had managed to follow for more than a day. The children grumbled about the new rules, Ben pretended not to see them, and Nadia herself had skipped the early walk she had promised. That evening they ordered pizza, and she sat at the table feeling that she had failed before she had properly begun.

Over the garden fence, their neighbour Mrs Obi, who had spent thirty years as a school nurse, listened to Nadia's story with a patient smile. She had seen countless families try to rebuild their lives in a single weekend, she said, and almost all of them were back where they started within a fortnight. What worked, in her experience, was far humbler: one small change at a time, repeated until it no longer felt like a change.

A habit, Mrs Obi explained, is simply an action repeated so many times that the brain stops treating it as a decision. You do not think about how to tie your shoes or where to find the kettle, because those steps have been filed away as automatic. That is a gift, since it leaves your attention free for harder things, but it also means that unhelpful routines can settle in just as quietly as helpful ones.

Habits, Mrs Obi went on, grow in particular places and at particular times, and they are set off by the ordinary signals of the day. Every afternoon, as soon as Ivy dropped her school bag in the hall, her hand travelled to the biscuit tin without waiting to be asked. Nobody had decided that this should happen, and that, Mrs Obi remarked, was exactly how a habit works.

Take that long list off the fridge, she advised, and choose only one thing from it, and make it so small that skipping it would feel almost silly. A glass of water, a five-minute walk or one extra vegetable would all be enough to begin with. The aim at this stage is not to improve your health overnight, but to prove to yourself that a new action can fit into an ordinary day.

At supper that evening, the four of them argued cheerfully about what the first step should be, until Ivy suggested water and nobody could think of a reason to say no. It was a modest choice, hardly the stuff of a family revolution, but its modesty was precisely the point. Everyone would drink one glass of water with breakfast, and for the moment the rest of the list could wait.

The trick, Mrs Obi told them, is to attach a new action to an old one that already happens every day without fail. The Carters never forgot to pour their cereal, so the glass of water was to follow the cereal every single morning, like a second carriage hooked behind a train. Because the old habit pulls the new one along, you do not have to rely on remembering.

Ben discovered that every small obstacle between a person and a good action makes it a little less likely to happen. So each night, before he went to bed, he filled a large jug with water and set it on the table beside four clean glasses. By morning the choice had been made for them, and drinking required no effort at all.

The first week was far from perfect, and on three mornings out of five Theo and Ivy poured their cereal and walked off without touching the water. Nadia felt the familiar sinking disappointment, but Mrs Obi, when she heard about it over the fence, was not in the least worried. A new habit is like a young seedling, she said, and nobody expects a seedling to stand firm in a strong wind.

Ivy, who took the matter very seriously, drew a chart with seven boxes and fixed it beside the fridge with a strip of tape. For every glass of water she added a gold star, and she made sure that everybody else's stars were visible too. Something about a row of bright stars, Nadia noticed, made it much harder to forget and much more satisfying to remember.

Mrs Obi described a celebrated piece of research in which volunteers chose a new daily action and then recorded how automatic it felt as the weeks went by. On average it took them about two months before the behaviour began to feel natural, but the spread was enormous, from a few weeks for some participants to the better part of a year for others. The moral, she said, is to be patient with yourself, and to remember that a single study cannot predict exactly how long your own family will need.

Once the glass of water had settled into the morning, Nadia felt confident enough to add a second small step, which was to decide the breakfasts a week ahead. On Sunday evening she wrote a short list, porridge with fruit on Monday, eggs on toast on Tuesday, and so on, and bought what was needed. A calm, planned breakfast turned out to be less about food than about removing a dozen small decisions from a hurried morning.

Looking at the shopping receipt, Nadia was startled by how many sweet drinks passed through the house in a single week. Fizzy drinks are made with a great deal of sugar, and even fruit juice, although it comes from fruit, can contain a surprising amount, so guidelines often suggest keeping both to small amounts. They did not ban anything, but they moved water and milk to the front of the shelf and let the sweet bottles drift to the back.

On Thursday, in the middle of a rush for the school bus, the entire family forgot the water, and one box on Ivy's chart stayed stubbornly empty. Ivy was close to tears, but Nadia knelt beside her and explained that a single gap does not undo a week of good mornings. What matters, she said, is not a perfect record but the willingness to begin again the very next day.

At the parents' evening in October, Theo's teacher mentioned, kindly, that he often seemed tired and sometimes struggled to keep his eyes open during the afternoon lessons. Nadia thought about the late nights that had crept in, the whispered conversations after lights-out and the glow of a tablet under the covers. It was becoming clear to her that the next small change ought to be about sleep, the least glamorous and perhaps the most important habit of all.

Nadia looked for reliable information and found that, according to major sleep organisations, children of Theo's age usually need between nine and twelve hours of sleep each night, while most adults do best with seven or more. Needs vary a little from one person to another, so these numbers are a guide rather than a law. Even so, Theo was getting closer to eight hours, which suggested that his yawns had a simple explanation.

Rather than simply announcing an earlier bedtime, the Carters built a short routine in which each step led naturally to the next. A bath was followed by teeth, teeth by a story, and the story by lights out, always in the same order and at roughly the same time. Repetition gave the evening a gentle rhythm, so that the body began to expect sleep before the clock had even struck eight.

Research suggests that bright screens late in the evening, and the stimulating things we watch on them, can make it harder for some people to fall asleep, although the effect differs from person to person. The Carters did not wait to find out exactly how it affected them, and instead agreed to leave every phone and tablet in a basket in the hall at bedtime. The adults agreed to put theirs in the basket first, which, as Theo pointed out with some satisfaction, was only fair.

The parents realised, with a certain embarrassment, that the new bedtime rules applied to them as well, since they were often awake long after the children. Instead of a dramatic change, they agreed to turn off the lamp fifteen minutes earlier each week, until mornings began to feel easier. It was a patient way of moving a habit, a few small steps at a time, and it did not feel like a sacrifice.

One night in November, Theo lay awake for hours, and by morning he was convinced that the whole week was ruined. Nadia reassured him that an occasional poor night happens to everybody, and that the body is remarkably good at recovering when the routine stays steady. If sleep problems carry on for a long time, she added, the sensible step is to speak to a doctor, rather than to keep worrying alone.

Their next small step was to leave the car at home on Tuesdays and Thursdays and walk to school together, a journey of about twenty minutes. At first the children complained about the cold, but soon they were racing each other to the lamp posts and chatting about everything under the sky. Ben, who had always been too busy for exercise, realised that he had just taken four thousand steps before nine o'clock.

Health organisations, Nadia learned, generally advise that children should be active for about an hour a day on average, and that adults should aim for around 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, such as brisk walking. These figures can sound daunting until you remember that movement can be gathered in small pieces throughout the day. Walking to school, climbing stairs and dancing in the kitchen all count towards the total.

After dinner, the Carters began to push back the sofa and put on music, and each evening a different member of the family chose the game. Ben's choice was a ridiculous version of musical statues, Theo preferred an energetic ball game, and Ivy always chose dancing. Nobody thought of it as exercise, which was exactly why it worked so well.

In winter, rain is the great enemy of every outdoor habit, and Nadia knew that a plan made only for fine weather would collapse by the second week. She therefore wrote a plan B on a card, which listed star jumps in the hallway, a stretching routine and a silly obstacle course made out of cushions. Having an alternative ready in advance meant that a grey day no longer ended in a day on the sofa.

Ivy looked at the little green trees on her plate and announced, with total conviction, that she hated broccoli and always would. Nadia felt the old urge to argue, bribe and bargain, but she remembered that pressure at the table often makes children dislike a food even more. So she said nothing at all, and the plate went quietly back to the kitchen.

Mrs Obi told her that many young children need to meet a new food a good many times before they will even taste it, and that this is a perfectly normal stage of growing up. The wise course, she said, is to offer a small piece calmly and regularly, to eat it yourself with obvious enjoyment, and to make no comment if it is left on the plate. It required more patience than cleverness, and Nadia found that she had plenty of the first.

On Saturday evening, Nadia handed the children their first real jobs in the kitchen, with Theo cutting cucumber under her watchful eye and Ivy washing tomatoes in a large bowl. It is often easier to get children interested in food they have helped to prepare, and the idea seemed to work, because both of them wanted to taste the salad before it reached the table. Even Ivy tried a small piece of green pepper, and the whole kitchen cheered.

A common piece of advice, repeated by many health authorities, is to eat at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day, though the exact recommendation varies a little from country to country. Rather than counting, the Carters turned it into a game in which each plate was supposed to show at least four colours, and whoever managed five won the right to choose the evening's music. The competition made vegetables feel less like a duty and more like a small adventure.

Nadia moved the fruit bowl from a forgotten corner to the middle of the kitchen table, and she shifted the sweets and biscuits to a high cupboard where they were out of sight. People tend to eat whatever is easiest to see and reach, she had read, whether or not they are truly hungry. The change cost nothing and required no willpower, yet within a week the apples were disappearing faster than ever.

Supper became the one fixed point of the day, when the whole family sat at the table, the screens stayed away and everybody had a chance to talk. Studies have often found that children who eat with their families a few times a week tend to do well, although it is hard to prove that the meals are the cause, since such families may differ in other ways. Whatever the research eventually shows, the Carters knew that they simply enjoyed one another's company more.

The real danger point, they found, was the late weekday evening, when everyone was tired and the takeaway menu seemed to glow like a lighthouse. So on Sunday afternoon Nadia cooked an enormous pot of vegetable soup and a tray of roasted vegetables, and Ben ladled them into boxes for the fridge. A healthy meal that needed only to be warmed up was, in practice, far more likely to be eaten than a healthy meal that still had to be planned.

When the winter holidays arrived, with their parties, puddings and late nights, the Carters made a deliberate decision not to fight the season. They ate the cake, stayed up past bedtime to watch a film and let the chart on the fridge gather dust for ten days. Mrs Obi had told them that a short break rarely undoes months of effort, and that what counts is returning to the routine afterwards, without guilt or drama.

January brought a mountain of work, and Nadia noticed that she was snapping at the children over things that hardly mattered. Stress is a normal part of life, Mrs Obi reminded her, and the aim is not to remove it but to give yourself small ways of settling the body when it rises. Nadia tried taking three slow breaths with her hand on her stomach before answering, and although it was no miracle, she often found that her voice came out kinder.

At the close of supper, each member of the family took a turn to name one good thing and one difficult thing from the day, while the others listened attentively without hurrying to repair anything. Wellbeing is not only a matter of food, sleep and movement, Mrs Obi had said, but also of feeling heard, and a family that talks tends to notice trouble sooner. Ivy's good things were frequently about worms, and her difficulties were almost invariably about shoes.

Handwashing, Mrs Obi said, is among the simplest and most effective ways of stopping germs from travelling from one person to another. The Carters made it a habit before every meal and after every visit to the toilet, and the children sang a short song twice through to make sure they scrubbed for about twenty seconds. Soap and water are all that is needed, and it was the song, not the lecture, that made it stick.

Dentists generally advise brushing the teeth twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste, once last thing at night and once at another time of the day. The Carters tied the habit to the bedtime routine and the breakfast table, so that nobody had to remember it separately, and Ivy earned a sparkling tooth sticker for every brush. They also booked a visit to the dentist, because regular check-ups can catch small problems before they grow.

As the days grew longer and warmer, Mrs Obi reminded the family that the sun, however pleasant, can damage the skin, and that children's skin is especially delicate. The sensible precautions are simple: look for shade around the middle of the day, wear a hat and light clothing, and apply sun cream before going outside. Ben kept a bottle by the front door, so that the habit began with the simple act of opening it.

On the calendar, in a different colour, Nadia wrote the dates of the children's routine check-ups and vaccinations, and she followed the advice of the family doctor and the local nurse. Recommended vaccines differ from one country to another, so general books cannot tell you exactly which ones your child needs. Good habits can support health, but they work alongside medical care and never replace it.

Rules that arrive from above, Nadia suspected, would be broken as soon as her back was turned, so the family held a meeting at which everybody helped to write a plan for daytime screens. They agreed on screen-free meals, an hour of play outside before any games, and a quiet time before supper, and the adults promised to obey the same rules. Because the children had a hand in making them, they were remarkably keen to enforce them.

In March a nasty cold passed from child to parent and back again, and for a whole week every new habit vanished beneath tissues, soup and daytime television. When they recovered, Nadia felt the old sinking feeling, but Mrs Obi told her that a routine you have built before is much easier to rebuild than one you have never had. She advised them to restart with the smallest step, the glass of water, and to let the rest return in its own time.

Nadia began to see the house as a stage that quietly shapes everyone's behaviour, for better or worse. Walking shoes were placed beside the front door, a water bottle sat on every school bag, and a football lay on a low shelf where the children could not miss it. The best plan, she realised, was not to rely on willpower, which runs out by the end of a long day, but to arrange the surroundings so that the healthy choice was the easy one.

Nadia worried that healthy food was a luxury, until Mrs Obi pointed out that some of the most nourishing foods are among the cheapest in the shop. Frozen vegetables are usually frozen soon after they are picked and can be as nutritious as fresh ones, and dried beans, lentils and oats are filling, inexpensive and keep for months. Not every family has the same time, money or energy, she added, and it is perfectly fine to do what is possible for your own.

Nadia noticed that Ivy copied everything the adults did, from the way they drank their water to the way they sat down to eat, and that Theo watched Ben's slow, wobbly jogs with open interest. Children learn far more from what they see than from what they are told, Mrs Obi observed, so the best lesson is a quiet example repeated every day. It was an encouraging thought, though also a slightly alarming one, since the children saw the bad habits as well.

In the spring, Theo came home from school with a poster for a fun run in July, a two-kilometre course through the park, and announced that he was going to run it. Nadia was delighted, but she was careful to keep the plan gentle, with a few short, easy runs a week that grew only a little longer each time. A goal, she explained to him, works best when it is made of small steps, because the steps are what you actually do.

Theo marked a green tick on the wall calendar after every run, and before long the rest of the family wanted ticks of their own for walks, dances and bicycle rides. A visible record of progress is satisfying, and it is a gentle reminder on the days when motivation is low. The Carters, however, took care to treat the calendar as a friend rather than a judge, and a day without a tick was simply a day without a tick.

Mrs Obi was careful to say that habits are helpful, but they are not magic, and they do not explain everything about a person's health. Illness, genes, poverty, long working hours and bad luck all play their parts, and none of them is anybody's fault. Anyone who is worried about a child's growth, sleep, mood or health, she insisted, should talk to a doctor or nurse, rather than rely on a book or a neighbour, however kind.

On a bright morning in July, Theo ran the whole two kilometres, red in the face and grinning, while Ben, Nadia and Ivy cheered at the finish line as if he had won a world championship. Later, on the grass, Nadia added up the year in her head: water at breakfast, a calmer bedtime, walks to school, more colour on the plate. Not one of these changes had been dramatic, but together they had quietly changed how the family lived.

In the evening light, Mrs Obi told Nadia to choose one small next step, to keep going when life gets in the way, and to be as kind to herself as to a friend. This book has offered only general information about everyday habits, and it is not medical advice, so it can never replace a doctor, nurse or dentist who knows you and your family. If you have a worry about your own health or your child's, please speak to a qualified professional, and then perhaps pour yourself a glass of water.
